d.title: The same protocol, three pipes - and the defaults that matter
d.caption: **The messages are identical in all three cases** — same JSON-RPC, same methods, same handshake — so the transport is one argument to `mcp.run` and nothing about a tool changes. **Note `host` defaulting to `127.0.0.1`:** a server started with no arguments is reachable only from the same machine, which is the right default and the first thing people change without weighing it. Two paths for SSE against one for streamable HTTP is the architectural difference, visible in the defaults.

d.title: Four things stdio gives you, and the one it cannot
d.caption: **The strongest access control in the course, and it costs nothing:** the server is a child process, nothing else on the machine is talking to it, and there is no port to find. The flip side is the trust it demands — configuring a stdio server means telling your host to run a command, which is the same decision as installing a dependency, so pin it and never build the command from user input. **And the last row is the hard limit:** it cannot cross a machine.

steps.code: a lifespan that means one thing
state: one caller, so one connection is right
there is one caller - the launcher

steps.code: but it cannot cross a machine
state: no shared service, no load balancer

d.title: Different session ids, the same pid
d.caption: **Compare with stdio's 10152 and 22540: the isolation has moved from the operating system to a string in a header.** Everything that was free is now your responsibility — and the lifespan row is the one that breaks previously-correct code. A single database connection or a mutable cache that was per-caller under stdio now serves everyone, producing concurrency bugs that are load-dependent and absent from every test that connects one client.

state: a session id, in ONE process

d.title: A session id, or none at all
d.caption: **Most MCP servers are request-response and need no session**: a tool takes arguments and returns a result, with nothing to remember. For those, stateless plus `json_response` makes the server behave like every other service you run — any replica, any load balancer, no affinity to get wrong. **Keep the session only when you need server-initiated messages**, and then accept the usual consequences: sticky routing or shared session storage, and a decision about a replica restarting mid-conversation.

d.title: Choosing, and why starting with stdio costs you nothing
d.caption: **Nothing about a tool's implementation changes between transports** — the decorators, the schemas and the error handling are identical, and the transport is one argument. So writing a server over stdio and moving it later is a small change, **provided you revisit the lifespan**: that is the one place where the transport reaches back into the server's design.

d.title: Mount it under your app, not the other way round
d.caption: **`streamable_http_app()` returns a mountable ASGI app**, so the MCP endpoint becomes one route in an application you own. The immediate reason is a health check — a load balancer needs something cheap to poll, and a POST carrying an `initialize` is a poor liveness probe. **The larger reason is that middleware on your app runs before the MCP endpoint sees anything**, and that is where authentication has to live. A server that mounts itself leaves you nowhere to stand.

d.title: The rejection has to precede the handshake
d.caption: **By the time a tool body runs, the caller has already read your entire tool list and every description in it.** So a check inside each tool stops the call and not the reconnaissance — and it has to be remembered in every tool including the one added next month. Middleware rejects before any MCP message is parsed, which is the property worth having. **But note the last node:** a bearer token authenticates the client, not a user, so a server with a token check feels secured and has not solved what a multi-user deployment needs.

d.title: On by default, and measured
d.caption: **Protection is on with empty allow-lists, and the empty list is a statement rather than a gap:** no browser origin is permitted, while ordinary server-to-server calls carrying no Origin keep working. The attack is specific to local servers — a hostile page the user visits makes requests to `127.0.0.1`, and without the check it can drive every tool with the user's own access. **When a legitimate caller gets a 403, add its host to the allow-list**; disabling the protection is the one change that opens a local server to any page.

d.title: Four ways a stream stops being one
d.caption: **Every one of these is invisible locally, because nothing sits between the client and the server.** The production symptom is an agent that works and is inexplicably slow, with no error logged by anything — which is why the honest check is a tool that reports progress for sixty seconds, called through the deployed URL. Either the updates arrive as they are sent or something in the chain is buffering, and knowing which takes one minute.

d.title: Seven things a server says, all of them in the model's context
d.caption: **A tool description is in the same position as a retrieved document: untrusted text the model will read and may act on.** Two asymmetries make it worse than ordinary injection. It requires only that someone install the server, rather than getting a document into a retrieval corpus — and it arrives *before* any user message, in the system-adjacent part of the context where models weight instructions most heavily. **It is also persistent:** resent on every request for the life of the connection, with nothing in the conversation looking unusual.

d.title: Four attacks, and what each one exploits
d.caption: **None of these requires the server to be malicious** — a compromised dependency, a careless maintainer or an ordinary feature update produces the same effect. The rug pull is the one that defeats reviewing descriptions, because it changes them after you read them. **And shadowing follows from the architecture rather than a bug:** lesson 1.1 measured that the host merges tool lists and a server cannot see its neighbours, so nothing is positioned to deny a claim about another server's tools.

state: none of it is content filtering

d.title: Seven controls, ranked by whether they survive the server changing
d.caption: **Reading the descriptions is necessary and insufficient, because the rug pull defeats it by construction.** An allow-list inverts that: a tool you did not name is not callable whatever the server does next, and the list is a short artefact a reviewer can question in a pull request. **It is also the fix for the accuracy problem from lesson 1.1**, so the security change and the quality change are one line. And the last row bounds everything — what the agent cannot do, it cannot be persuaded into.

d.title: Naming the untrusted field helps, and is not a boundary
d.caption: **A tool that reads a support ticket returns text a member of the public typed**, and marking which field that is measurably helps while costing almost nothing. What it cannot do is make your note privileged — both strings are text in one prompt with the same role. **So every control in this lesson is about consequences rather than content:** you cannot make a description trustworthy, you cannot reliably detect an instruction hidden in a result, and a classifier that tries is wrong in both directions.

nodes.label: So secure the CONSEQUENCES

d.title: Five things an author owes a consumer
d.caption: **A description that reads like a prompt makes your server indistinguishable from a poisoned one**, which is the first row's real argument. **And the second is the one people treat as a courtesy:** a new tool is a change to every consumer's prompt, so shipping one silently is exactly the behaviour a rug pull relies on — which makes a changelog and a version bump a security contribution. Stable names matter for the same reason: renaming tools between releases makes the one effective control painful to maintain, which discourages its use.
